title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
Welcome
I wrote this tutorial because most PLINK material is written for human genetics. The ideas are the same in cattle, sheep and goats, but the details are not: we have 29 cattle autosomes instead of 22, we have big half-sib families, we mix breeds, and our pedigrees are often wrong. Every example here uses livestock data, and every output you see was produced by actually running the command shown.

title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
The data
We use two kinds of data.
A simulated cattle dataset (361 animals of three breeds, 4,800 SNPs). Because it was simulated, we know the truth: I hid lab errors (bad samples, a duplicate, a wrong sire, sex mix-ups, strand flips) and real genetic effects in it, and the chapters show how PLINK finds each one.
Two real public datasets: 500 genotyped cattle with a pedigree (from the synbreedData R package) and 100 sheep of two breeds, Jacob and Navajo-Churro, published by Kijas and colleagues (2016) and shipped with the detectRUNS R package. These show what real data look like, which is always a little messier than a simulation.
Everything is in the data/ and scripts/ folders of the GitHub repository, so you can repeat every step.

title: PLINK for Livestock Genomics
text:
Which PLINK?
PLINK has three versions that are still in use. This book uses PLINK 1.9 for almost everything, gives the PLINK 2.0 command in a blue box, and uses PLINK 1.07 only for the old tools that newer versions dropped (haplotype tests and CNV analysis). Chapter 1 explains the differences.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
text:
1.1 What PLINK is
Picture a giant spreadsheet. Each row is an animal, each column is a SNP, and each cell holds two letters, one inherited from the sire and one from the dam (for example A G). A 50K chip gives 50,000 columns; a high-density chip gives 777,000. No spreadsheet program can open that. PLINK can. It reads the genotypes, checks their quality, counts things, compares groups of animals and writes small result tables that you can open in R or Excel.

text:
1.4 Step 2: unzip and put it somewhere sensible
Create one folder for your genomics work, for example C:/genomics on Windows or ~/genomics on macOS and Linux, and unzip PLINK there. Put your data in the same folder at first. Later, when you are comfortable, you can add PLINK to your PATH so that it runs from any folder.

WindowsmacOSLinux



Unzip the file into C:\genomics.
Open Command Prompt (press the Windows key, type cmd, press Enter).
Move into your folder and test PLINK:

cd C:\genomics
plink --version
To run PLINK from any folder, add C:\genomics to your PATH: search for “Edit the system environment variables”, click Environment Variables, select Path, click Edit, then New, and paste C:\genomics.



Unzip the file into ~/genomics (a folder called genomics in your home folder).
Open Terminal (Applications, Utilities).
Make the file executable and test it:

cd ~/genomics
chmod +x plink
./plink --version
The first time, macOS may refuse to open a program from an “unidentified developer”. Either right-click the file in Finder and choose Open, or run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine plink once in the terminal.


mkdir -p ~/genomics && cd ~/genomics
unzip plink_linux_x86_64_*.zip
chmod +x plink
./plink --version
# optional: make it available everywhere
sudo cp plink /usr/local/bin/



If you see a line such as PLINK v1.9..., you are ready. On macOS and Linux, ./plink means “the plink in this folder”. Once PLINK is on your PATH, you can type just plink.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
text:
1.6 Anatomy of a PLINK command
Every PLINK command has three parts: what to read, what to do, and where to write.
plink --bfile cattle --cow --geno 0.05 --make-bed --out cattle_clean
#      \___ read ___/ \_______ do ________/ \___ write ___/

--bfile cattle reads the three files cattle.bed, cattle.bim and cattle.fam. You give the name without the extension.
Words starting with two dashes are flags. Some take a value (--geno 0.05); some do not (--cow).
--out cattle_clean sets the start of every output file name. Without it, PLINK calls everything plink.* and overwrites your earlier results.
The order of flags on the line does not matter. PLINK decides the order of operations itself (Chapter 6 shows why this matters).
crumbs: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
section: 1.7 The log file is your best friend
text:
1.7 The log file is your best friend
Every run writes a .log file with the same name as the output (cattle_clean.log). It repeats your command and reports what happened: how many animals and SNPs were read, how many were removed and why, and any warnings. Get into the habit of reading it every time. PLINK usually does exactly what you asked, which is not always what you meant, and the log is where you find out.

title: 1  Installing PLINK and running your first command
section: 1.8 The flag every livestock user needs: --cow
text:
1.8 The flag every livestock user needs: --cow
PLINK was written for humans. By default it expects chromosomes 1 to 22, and it reads code 23 as X, 24 as Y, 25 as the pseudo-autosomal region (XY) and 26 as mitochondria. Cattle have 29 autosomes. This is what happened when I loaded our cattle file without telling PLINK the species:
Error: Invalid chromosome code '27' on line 4101 of .map file.
(This is disallowed for humans.  Check if the problem is with your data, or if
you forgot to define a different chromosome set with e.g. --chr-set.)
That error is the lucky case. If your file only had chromosomes up to 26, PLINK would have read cattle chromosome 23 as the X and chromosome 24 as the Y without complaining, and your sex checks and association results would be quietly wrong.

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.1 Step 1: install R, RStudio and a few packages
There is no “PLINK package” that replaces the PLINK program. In R we do one of two things: we call the PLINK program from R, or we read PLINK’s files into R. This chapter shows both.

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
section: 2.3 Step 3: get PLINK into the project
text:
2.3 Step 3: get PLINK into the project
You have three choices. Use whichever works on your computer.
Option A: download it by hand (Chapter 1) and copy the file into the project folder.
Option B: let R download it. The bigsnpr package has helper functions that download the right PLINK build for your system and return its path:
library(bigsnpr)
plink  <- download_plink(dir = ".")     # PLINK 1.9
plink2 <- download_plink2(dir = ".")    # PLINK 2.0
plink                                    # prints the full path, e.g. "./plink"
Option C: use the RStudio Terminal. RStudio has a Terminal tab next to the Console. It is a normal command line that opens in your project folder, so every command in this book works there unchanged.
crumbs: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.4 Step 4: run PLINK from R
R’s system2() function runs an outside program. Give it the program path and the arguments:
plink <- "./plink"           # on Windows: "plink.exe"

system2(plink, args = c("--file", "data/cattle", "--cow",
                        "--make-bed", "--out", "results/cattle"))
The older system() function takes the whole command as one string, which is handy for copying commands from this book:
system("./plink --bfile results/cattle --cow --missing --out results/miss")
On Windows, write paths with forward slashes ("C:/genomics/plink.exe") or doubled backslashes ("C:\\genomics\\plink.exe"). A single backslash breaks the string.
A small helper function saves typing and prints PLINK’s messages in the Console:
run_plink <- function(..., exe = "./plink") {
  args <- c(...)
  out <- system2(exe, args = args, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)
  cat(out, sep = "\n")
  invisible(out)
}

run_plink("--bfile", "results/cattle", "--cow", "--freq", "--out", "results/freq")
crumbs: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio

section: 2.5 Step 5: read the results into R
text:
2.5 Step 5: read the results into R
Almost every PLINK output is a plain text table with a header line and columns separated by spaces. read.table(header = TRUE) reads it, and data.table::fread() does the same faster for big files.
library(tidyverse)

imiss <- read.table("results/miss.imiss", header = TRUE)
lmiss <- read.table("results/miss.lmiss", header = TRUE)

ggplot(imiss, aes(x = F_MISS * 100)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#E69F00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Missing genotypes per animal (%)", y = "Number of animals",
       title = "Missingness per animal") +
  theme_minimal()

library(genio)
geno <- read_plink("results/cattle")

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
section: 2.6 Step 6: let a package do routine QC for you
text:
2.6 Step 6: let a package do routine QC for you
The plinkQC package by Hannah Meyer wraps PLINK’s QC commands (missingness, heterozygosity, sex check, relatedness) and makes clear plots. It follows the QC protocol of Anderson and colleagues (2010).
library(plinkQC)
fail_miss_het <- check_het_and_miss(indir = "results", name = "human_data",
                                     path2plink = "./plink", interactive = TRUE)
It was written for human data and calls PLINK without a species flag, so with cattle files PLINK stops at chromosome codes above 26. For livestock I use it as a model: run the PLINK commands from this book with --cow, then copy its plotting ideas into your own ggplot code.
crumbs: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio

title: 2  Using PLINK from R and RStudio
text:
2.7 Keep a record
Write your commands in an R script or a Quarto notebook rather than typing them into the Console. Six months later, when a reviewer asks “which --geno threshold did you use?”, the answer is in the file, together with the plot it produced.






WarningCommon mistake



If system2() returns status 127 or “cannot find”, R is not looking where PLINK is. Check with file.exists(plink), and on macOS or Linux make the file executable once with Sys.chmod(plink, mode = "0755").

title: 3  Genotype files: what PLINK reads and writes
text:
3.2 The binary format: .bed, .bim and .fam
Text files are huge (each genotype takes four characters: two letters and two spaces) and slow to read. PLINK’s binary format stores each genotype in 2 bits, so our practice file shrank from 6.9 MB to 0.44 MB, and PLINK reads it many times faster. Convert first, and then always work with the binary files.
plink --file cattle --cow --make-bed --out cattle

.fam is the first six columns of the .ped.
.bim is the .map plus two extra columns: allele 1 (A1) and allele 2 (A2).
.bed holds the genotypes. It is not text, so do not open it in an editor.

cattle.bim:  1   snp00001   0.484    484050   G   A
             1   snp00002   2.2237   2223660  C   A






WarningA1 is not “the reference allele”



PLINK 1.9 makes A1 the minor (rarer) allele by default. Every effect size PLINK reports (odds ratio, beta) is for A1. If you need A1 to be a fixed allele, for example the reference allele of the genome assembly, add --keep-allele-order or set it with --a1-allele (Chapter 5). PLINK 2.0 keeps the input order and calls the alleles REF and ALT.

The additive .raw file is the one you will use most for your own models. Each genotype column counts copies of the allele named in the header:

So snp00004_T = 1 means ANG_001 carries one T at that SNP. Missing genotypes appear as NA.

section: 3.4 Extra files: phenotypes, covariates and clusters
text:
3.4 Extra files: phenotypes, covariates and clusters
Real projects keep traits and covariates in separate files. All of them start with FID and IID:
pheno.txt     FID IID WWT BW YWT BRD
              ANG ANG_001 265.0 38.8 523.1 1
covar.txt     FID IID SEX_M FEEDLOT AGE HERD_N
              ANG ANG_001 0 0 215 1
breed.clst    ANG ANG_001 ANG          (cluster file: no header, third column = group)
You point PLINK to them with --pheno, --covar and --within. Missing values are -9 everywhere unless you change the code with --missing-phenotype.






TipLook before you analyse



head cattle.fam and head cattle.bim take two seconds. Check that sexes are 1 and 2 (not M and F), that phenotypes look sensible, and that chromosome codes are numbers your species flag accepts.

title: 4  The practice data
text:
4.2 The simulated cattle
The cattle were simulated with a Python script (scripts/simulate.py, random seed 2026), so the truth is known. Positions and gene names such as PLAG1 and LCORL are used only as labels to make the story easier to follow; the effects are invented.







Item
What is in the data




Breeds
Angus (ANG), Holstein (HOL), N’Dama (NDA), with different allele frequencies


Animals
361: 240 unrelated (80 per breed), 30 families of sire + dam + 2 calves (15 Holstein, 15 N’Dama), and 1 repeated sample


Sex
137 males, 222 females, 2 unknown


SNPs
4,800: 150 per autosome on chromosomes 1 to 29, extra-dense regions on chromosomes 5, 6 and 14, and 250 on the X


Disease (column 6 of .ped)
BRD, bovine respiratory disease: 144 cases (2), 217 controls (1)


Measured traits (pheno.txt)
WWT weaning weight (kg), BW birth weight (kg), YWT yearling weight (kg)


Covariates (covar.txt)
SEX_M (1 = male), FEEDLOT (1 = feedlot, 0 = pasture), AGE at weaning (days), HERD_N


Other files

4.2.1 The hidden problems
These are the things the simulation planted. Try to find them yourself before reading the answer key in Chapter 19.

Some SNPs fail often in the lab, and six animals have poor-quality DNA.
One animal was genotyped twice, and one DNA sample was contaminated with another animal’s DNA.
Two bulls are recorded as cows, and two animals have no recorded sex.
One calf has the wrong sire in the pedigree.
One animal is highly inbred, one is a crossbred and one is labelled with the wrong breed.
Some SNPs have calling errors that break Hardy-Weinberg and Mendel’s laws.
Some SNPs fail more often in sick animals than in healthy ones.
The second lab reported 40 SNPs on the opposite DNA strand.
Real effects: two weaning-weight QTL, one BRD risk SNP, one SNP that only matters in the feedlot, and a CNV deletion linked to BRD.

title: 5  Converting, subsetting and merging data

plink --file cattle --cow --make-bed --out cattle
Scanning .ped file... done.
Performing single-pass .bed write (4800 variants, 361 cattle).
361 cattle (137 males, 222 females, 2 ambiguous) loaded from .fam.
Warning: Ignoring phenotypes of missing-sex samples.  If you don't want those
phenotypes to be ignored, use the --allow-no-sex flag.
Before main variant filters, 301 founders and 60 nonfounders present.
Warning: 9 het. haploid genotypes present (see cattle.hh ); many commands
treat these as missing.
Total genotyping rate is 0.992812.
4800 variants and 361 cattle pass filters and QC.
Among remaining phenotypes, 144 are cases and 217 are controls.


137 males, 222 females, 2 ambiguous: “ambiguous” means sex code 0. Their IDs go to cattle.nosex.
Ignoring phenotypes of missing-sex samples: PLINK 1.9 leaves those two animals out of association tests unless you add --allow-no-sex. Chapter 17 shows the difference it makes.
301 founders and 60 nonfounders: a founder has both parents unknown. Our 60 calves are nonfounders. Allele frequencies and Hardy-Weinberg tests use founders only, so that a sire’s alleles are not counted again in each of his calves.
9 het. haploid genotypes: a bull has one X chromosome, so he cannot be heterozygous on the X. When he looks heterozygous, it is a genotyping error (a few are normal) or a sex error (hundreds in one animal). The file cattle.hh lists them.
Total genotyping rate is 0.992812: 99.3% of all genotype cells are filled in.

5.4 Step 4: merge files from two labs
Merging adds new animals as rows and new SNPs as columns. The classic trap is the DNA strand. DNA has two strands that pair A with T and C with G. If one lab reports a SNP as A/G and the other reads the opposite strand, it reports T/C for the same SNP, and PLINK sees four alleles.

  A[File 1 and File 2] --> B["plink --bmerge"]
  B -->|works| C[merged file]
  B -->|"Error: 3+ alleles"| D["SNP list in *-merge.missnp"]
  D --> E["--flip on File 2"]
  E --> B
  C --> F["Remove A/T and C/G SNPs<br/>and check with --flip-scan"]






 The merge workflow. The loop through –flip is usually needed once. 



Our second lab sent 40 animals and 4,200 SNPs, with 40 SNPs on the opposite strand:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2 --make-bed --out merged_try1
40 cattle to be merged from batch2.fam.
Of these, 40 are new, while 0 are present in the base dataset.
4200 markers to be merged from batch2.bim.
Of these, 120 are new, while 4080 are present in the base dataset.
Error: 39 variants with 3+ alleles present.
* If you believe this is due to strand inconsistency, try --flip with
  merged_try1-merge.missnp.
Flip those SNPs in the second file and merge again:
plink --bfile batch2 --cow --flip merged_try1-merge.missnp --make-bed --out batch2_flipped
plink --bfile cattle --cow --allow-no-sex --bmerge batch2_flipped --make-bed --out merged
# 4920 variants and 401 cattle pass filters and QC.
PLINK caught 39 of the 40. The missing one, snp03921, is a C/G SNP: flipping C/G gives G/C, the same two letters, so no error is raised and the alleles are silently swapped. A/T SNPs behave the same way. That is why the safe practice is:

Remove strand-ambiguous SNPs (A/T and C/G) before merging data from different sources. Our file had 143 of them:
awk '($5=="A"&&$6=="T")||($5=="T"&&$6=="A")||($5=="C"&&$6=="G")||($5=="G"&&$6=="C"){print $2}' cattle.bim > ambiguous.txt
Better still, ask both labs to export with the same allele coding (Illumina TOP or Forward strand).
Run --flip-scan, which looks for SNPs whose LD with their neighbours has the wrong sign. It needs strong LD, so on our sparse SNPs it flagged 6 SNPs and missed snp03921. It is useful on dense chips.

Two more things the merge taught us. Without --allow-no-sex, PLINK refused to write the merged file because two animals had unknown sex. And SNPs typed by only one lab are missing for every animal of the other lab, so run --geno (Chapter 6) after every merge.

title: 6  Missing genotypes: per SNP and per animal
text:
6.1 Why genotypes go missing
A SNP chip measures two light signals per SNP. When the signals are clear, the calling software assigns AA, AB or BB. When they are weak or fall between the clusters, it gives up and writes 0 0. This happens for two quite different reasons.
So we measure missingness in two directions:
\[
\text{missing rate of an animal} = \frac{\text{SNPs with no genotype in that animal}}{\text{all SNPs}}
\qquad
\text{missing rate of a SNP} = \frac{\text{animals with no genotype at that SNP}}{\text{all animals}}
\]
The call rate is just one minus the missing rate: an animal with 2% missing has a 98% call rate.

title: 6  Missing genotypes: per SNP and per animal
text:
The animal’s DNA is poor (degraded, too little, contaminated). Then many SNPs fail in that one animal.
The SNP’s probe works badly (it sits near another variant, or in a repeated region). Then that one SNP fails in many animals.

section: 6.2 The logic, with a toy example
text:
6.2 The logic, with a toy example
The two directions are tangled: every missing cell counts against one animal and one SNP. That is why the order of filtering matters. Here is a small table of six animals and eight SNPs. Genotypes are written the way Illumina reports them: AA, AB or BB, with -- for a call that failed.






Figure 6.1: Case 1: one failed SNP. SNP3 could not be read in four animals, so those four look poor. Dropping that SNP first brings three of them back to 0%.



In case 1, the probe for SNP3 failed in four of the six animals (67% missing). That single SNP pushes Animals 1, 3 and 4 to 12% missing and Animal 2 to 25%. If we filtered animals first with, say, a 10% cut-off, we would discard four animals because of one bad probe. Drop SNP3 first and three of them are perfect; Animal 2 keeps one genuine gap (1 of 7 SNPs, 14%).
Now the opposite situation:






Figure 6.2: Case 2: one failed sample. Animal 4’s DNA could not be read at six SNPs, so six SNPs look 17% missing. Dropping the animal first brings every SNP back to 0%.



In case 2, Animal 4’s sample failed at six of eight SNPs (75%). In a table of only six animals, that one sample makes six SNPs look 17% missing. Filter SNPs first and we lose six good SNPs; drop the animal first and every SNP is back to 0%.
The rule behind both cases: a bad SNP inflates every animal’s rate, and a bad animal inflates every SNP’s rate. How much depends on the size of the table. On a chip with 50,000 SNPs, one failed SNP adds only 0.002% to each animal. In a study of a few hundred animals, one failed sample adds a visible amount to every SNP. So in livestock studies, which usually have far more SNPs than animals, bad animals are the bigger threat to SNP call rates.
A practical plan follows from this. First remove only the disasters, with a lenient cut-off in both directions. Then apply the strict cut-offs, animals before SNPs, so that a few bad samples cannot drag good SNPs over the line.

  B --> C["Round 2: --mind 0.03<br/>(animals, strict)"]
  C --> D["--geno 0.01<br/>(SNPs, strict)"]
  D --> E[clean data]






 A two-round missingness filter. The lenient round removes only the obvious failures; the strict round handles animals before SNPs.

title: 7  Allele frequency and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
text:
7.1 Allele frequency and MAF
At every SNP each animal carries two copies, so 100 animals carry 200 allele copies. The allele frequency is the share of those copies that carry a given allele. The rarer of the two alleles is the minor allele, and its frequency is the minor allele frequency (MAF).
A worked example. Eight animals have these genotypes at one SNP: CT, TT, CC, TT, TT, CT, TT, TT.
So p(C) = 4/16 = 0.25 and p(T) = 12/16 = 0.75. C is the minor allele, and MAF = 0.25. A SNP with MAF = 0 is monomorphic: every animal has the same genotype, so it tells us nothing about differences between animals.

title: 7  Allele frequency and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
text:
7.2 Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)
If animals mate at random and nothing else disturbs a SNP, genotype frequencies follow a fixed rule from the allele frequencies p and q = 1 - p:
\[
P(AA) = p^2, \qquad P(AG) = 2pq, \qquad P(GG) = q^2
\]
Take a SNP where p(A) = 0.3 and q(G) = 0.7. The expected shares are 0.3² = 0.09, 2 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.42 and 0.7² = 0.49, so in 100 animals we expect 9 AA, 42 AG and 49 GG.






Figure 7.2: A SNP with too few heterozygotes. Observed counts (orange) differ strongly from Hardy-Weinberg expectations (grey).



The observed counts in the figure (20, 20, 60) give exactly the same allele frequency (A = (2 × 20 + 20) / 200 = 0.3), but only half the expected heterozygotes and more than twice the expected AA animals. A classic cause is a genotype-calling error in which the calling software misses heterozygotes. PLINK tests the departure with an exact test, which works well even for rare SNPs. A small p-value means the genotype counts are unlikely under HWE.
But genotyping errors are not the only cause of departure from HWE. Selection, inbreeding, a deletion on the SNP, and above all mixing populations also do it. That last one is the important trap in livestock.

7.2.1 Step 3: run the test
plink --bfile cattle --cow --hardy --out hwe

   1   snp00001      AFF    G    A              0/3/116  0.02521  0.02489            1
   1   snp00001    UNAFF    G    A             0/12/168  0.06667  0.06444            1
Each SNP gets three lines: all animals (ALL), cases (AFF) and controls (UNAFF). GENO is the count of hom A1 / het / hom A2; O(HET) and E(HET) are observed and expected heterozygosity. Why three lines? A SNP that really causes a disease can be out of HWE in cases for a genuine biological reason. That is why the --hwe filter in PLINK 1.9 uses controls only when a case/control phenotype is present.


7.2.2 Step 4: watch out for the Wahlund effect
When you pool breeds that have different allele frequencies, you always see fewer heterozygotes than expected, even if each breed is perfectly in HWE. This is called the Wahlund effect. Picture one breed where nearly all animals are AA and another where nearly all are GG. Pool them and the “population” has an allele frequency near 0.5, so HWE expects about half the animals to be AG, but almost none are.

8.1 Heterozygosity and inbreeding
Every animal has an expected number of homozygous genotypes, given the allele frequencies in the population. PLINK compares observed and expected homozygosity with the inbreeding coefficient F:
\[
F = \frac{O(\text{HOM}) - E(\text{HOM})}{N - E(\text{HOM})}
\]
where O(HOM) is the observed number of homozygous SNPs, E(HOM) the expected number and N the number of SNPs with a genotype.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.1 Where LD comes from
When a mutation first appears, it sits on one particular chromosome with one particular set of alleles around it. Every copy of the mutation in later generations descends from that first copy, so at first it always comes with the same neighbours. Each generation, recombination swaps pieces between the two chromosomes of a parent. A SNP 10 Mb away is separated from the mutation quickly; a SNP 10 kb away almost never. So LD is strong between nearby SNPs and weak between distant ones.
In livestock, LD extends much further than in humans, because breeds were founded from few animals and a few popular sires have many offspring (a small effective population size). That is why 50,000 SNPs are enough for genomic selection in cattle.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text: Figure 9.1: A new mutation appears on one chromosome. Over generations, recombination cuts the chromosome, but the pieces right next to the mutation are rarely separated from it.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.2 Haplotypes
A haplotype is the set of alleles on one chromosome copy. With two SNPs, one with alleles A/C and one with alleles G/T, there are four possible haplotypes: A-G, A-T, C-G and C-T. Each animal carries two haplotypes, one from each parent.
From genotypes alone we often cannot tell which haplotypes an animal has. An animal that is A/C at the first SNP and G/T at the second could carry A-G + C-T, or A-T + C-G. Finding the right pair is called phasing. PLINK estimates haplotype frequencies statistically, and dedicated programs such as BEAGLE and SHAPEIT phase whole chromosomes.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
section: 9.3 Measuring LD: D, D′ and r²
text:
9.3 Measuring LD: D, D′ and r²
Write fA for the frequency of allele A at SNP 1, fT for the frequency of allele T at SNP 2, and fAT for the frequency of the A-T haplotype. If the two SNPs were independent, the A-T haplotype frequency would simply be fA × fT. D measures how far reality is from that:
\[
D = f_{AT} - f_A \, f_T
\]
D depends on the allele frequencies, so two scaled versions are used:
\[
r^2 = \frac{D^2}{f_A(1-f_A)\,f_T(1-f_T)}
\qquad\qquad
D' = \frac{D}{D_{\max}}
\]
where Dmax is the largest value D could reach with these allele frequencies. r² is the squared correlation between the alleles; it ranges from 0 (independent) to 1 (one SNP perfectly predicts the other). D′ is 1 when at most three of the four haplotypes exist, even if one of them is rare. For association and genomic prediction, r² is the one to use: it tells you how well one SNP can stand in for another.

9.3.1 A worked example with real output
plink --bfile cattle --cow --ld snp02144 snp02145 --out ld_pair
   R-sq = 0.382072       D' = 0.642212

   Haplotype     Frequency    Expectation under LE
   ---------     ---------    --------------------
          AT      0.323442                0.173290
          CT      0.102233                0.252385
          AG      0.083652                0.233804
          CG      0.490672                0.340520

   In phase alleles are AT/CG
Let us check PLINK’s numbers by hand.

Allele frequencies: fA = AT + AG = 0.323 + 0.084 = 0.407, and fT = AT + CT = 0.323 + 0.102 = 0.426.
If independent, AT would be 0.407 × 0.426 = 0.173 (PLINK’s “expectation under LE”, linkage equilibrium).
D = 0.323 − 0.173 = 0.150.
r² = 0.150² / (0.407 × 0.593 × 0.426 × 0.574) = 0.0225 / 0.0590 = 0.382. ✔
Dmax = min(0.407 × 0.574, 0.593 × 0.426) = 0.234, so D′ = 0.150 / 0.234 = 0.642. ✔

“In phase alleles are AT/CG” means A tends to travel with T, and C with G.






TipWhy r² can never reach 1 for some pairs



r² can only be 1 when the two SNPs have the same MAF. A SNP with MAF 0.05 and one with MAF 0.40 can never be perfectly correlated, however close they are. This is one reason rare variants are hard to tag with common chip SNPs.

title: 9  Linkage disequilibrium
text:
9.5 Why LD matters in practice
1. Tagging. A chip SNP does not need to be the causal mutation. If it is in strong LD with the causal variant, it shows the association for it. This is how genome-wide association works.
2. The top SNP is not necessarily causal. In Chapter 13 the weaning-weight signal appears at five SNPs in the PLAG1 region, because they are all in LD with each other. Separating the real cause from its neighbours is called fine-mapping. Conditional analysis (--condition, Chapter 13) is the PLINK tool for a first look.
3. Many analyses need independent SNPs. PCA, relatedness, F and admixture assume each SNP is a separate piece of evidence. In a block of ten SNPs in perfect LD, the region would count ten times. So we prune:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --autosome --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out prune
Pruned 82 variants from chromosome 14, leaving 148.
Pruning complete.  969 of 4550 variants removed.
--indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 looks at a window of 50 SNPs, removes one SNP from every pair with r² above 0.2, then slides the window 5 SNPs along and repeats. It writes prune.prune.in (SNPs to keep) and prune.prune.out; use them with --extract prune.prune.in. The heaviest pruning happened in the dense regions on chromosomes 14, 6 and 5, as expected. Chapter 17 shows how the three numbers change the result.
4. Summarising association results. --clump groups significant SNPs that are in LD with each other into one “clump” per signal, so that a list of 50 significant SNPs becomes, for example, 3 independent loci.






NotePLINK 2.0



plink2 --r2-unphased and --r2-phased replace --r2; --ld, --indep-pairwise and --clump work as in 1.9.

text:
10.1 IBS and IBD: two kinds of sharing
At any SNP, two animals can share 0, 1 or 2 alleles. There are two reasons they might share one.
IBD implies IBS, but not the other way round. Two unrelated Holsteins share many alleles by state simply because the alleles are common in Holsteins. Relatedness is about IBD.

Identical by state (IBS): the alleles are the same letter. That can happen by chance, especially for a common allele.
Identical by descent (IBD): the alleles are the same physical copy, inherited from a recent common ancestor.

text:
10.4 Step 2: the genomic relationship matrix (GRM)
A second way to measure relatedness treats each SNP as a small piece of evidence and averages over all SNPs. Write gil for the number of copies (0, 1 or 2) of allele 1 that animal i carries at SNP l, and fl for the frequency of that allele. The genomic relationship between animals i and j is
\[
\hat r_{ij} = \frac{1}{p}\sum_{l=1}^{p}\frac{(g_{il}-2f_l)(g_{jl}-2f_l)}{2f_l(1-f_l)}
\]
In words: standardise each genotype by subtracting its expected value and dividing by its standard deviation, then average the products over all p SNPs. Two animals that carry the same unusual alleles get a positive value; unrelated animals average about zero (and can be slightly negative). This is the GRM of Yang and colleagues (2011), used by GCTA and in GBLUP genomic prediction; VanRaden’s (2008) G matrix is a close relative.

# grm.rel     500 x 500 matrix of relationships

10.5 Step 3: KING, a method robust to structure
KING (Manichaikul and colleagues, 2010) estimates kinship without using population allele frequencies. It only looks at SNPs where both animals are heterozygous (NAa,Aa) and where they are opposite homozygotes (NAA,aa):

title: 10  Relatedness, inbreeding and runs of homozygosity
text:
10.6 Step 4: runs of homozygosity (ROH)
An inbred animal inherited the same long stretch of chromosome from both parents, because both got it from a common ancestor. That stretch shows up as a long run of homozygous SNPs, a run of homozygosity (ROH). The share of the genome covered by ROH is F_ROH, a genomic inbreeding coefficient widely used in livestock:
\[
F_{ROH} = \frac{\text{total length of ROH in the animal}}{\text{length of the genome covered by SNPs}}
\]
Long ROH come from recent inbreeding (the common ancestor was a few generations back); short ROH from old inbreeding. A common rule of thumb is that an ROH of length L cM traces back to a common ancestor about 50/L generations ago.

text:
11.1 The idea in two SNPs
Imagine only two SNPs, and plot every animal by its (standardised) genotype at SNP A and SNP B. If the two SNPs are correlated, the cloud of points is stretched along a diagonal.
PCA finds new axes for the same cloud:
Each PC is described by two things:
In the toy example, PC1 has eigenvalue 2.09 and PC2 only 0.14: PC1 carries 94% of the variation, so one number per animal describes almost everything the two SNPs say. With real data we do the same thing with thousands of SNPs at once.
crumbs: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
Figure 11.1: Left: animals plotted by two correlated SNPs. The red arrow (PC1) points along the direction where the animals differ most; the blue arrow (PC2) is at right angles to it. Right: the same animals after rotating the axes onto the PCs.





The first principal component (PC1) is the direction along which the animals differ the most.
PC2 is the direction of most remaining variation, at right angles to PC1, and so on.



An eigenvector: the direction itself, a list of weights, one per SNP (PLINK calls these the SNP loadings or variant weights). Projecting an animal onto that direction gives its PC score: the number you plot.
An eigenvalue: how much of the variation lies along that direction. A big eigenvalue means a PC that separates animals strongly.
crumbs: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.2 How PLINK computes it
PLINK first builds the genomic relationship matrix (GRM) from Chapter 10: one row and one column per animal, filled with the standardised genotype products averaged over SNPs. Then it finds the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of that matrix. Each eigenvector of the GRM has one value per animal: those values are the PC scores. In matrix language, if G is the GRM,
\[
\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{v}_k = \lambda_k\,\mathbf{v}_k
\]
where vk is the k-th eigenvector (the scores of all animals on PC k) and λk its eigenvalue. The eigenvalues add up to the total variation, which equals the sum of the diagonal of G (its trace, roughly the number of animals). So the share of variation explained by PC k is
\[
\text{\% variance of PC}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\text{trace}(\mathbf{G})} \times 100
\]






WarningThe most common PCA mistake



PLINK only writes the top 20 eigenvalues (or as many as you ask for). Many tutorials divide each eigenvalue by the sum of those values. That gives the share among the first few PCs, not of the total, and it exaggerates badly. In our data PC1 is 45% of the first ten eigenvalues but only 8.6% of the total variation. To get the true total, run --make-rel on the same SNPs and add up the diagonal (in R: sum(diag(G))), or use the number of animals as an approximation.

FID     IID       PC1        PC2        PC3
ANG     ANG_001   0.0118239  0.0913939  -0.00673676

32.9286

section: 11.5 Step 3: how many PCs matter? The scree plot
text:
11.5 Step 3: how many PCs matter? The scree plot






Figure 11.2: Scree plot. Bars show the share of the total variation (eigenvalue divided by 384.5, the trace of the GRM); numbers on the bars are the raw eigenvalues.



The first two eigenvalues (32.9 and 19.1) stand far above the rest, which flatten out near 2.5 to 2.9. That “elbow” after PC2 tells us there are two strong axes of structure: with three breeds, you need two axes to separate them (in general, k groups need k - 1 PCs). After the elbow, PCs mostly describe noise or small family groups. For association studies, people usually include the PCs up to the elbow, and often a few more for safety (Chapter 12 uses PC1 and PC2).

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.6 Step 4: plot the animals






Figure 11.3: PC1 against PC2 and PC1 against PC3, coloured by recorded breed. Axis labels give the share of the total variation.




PC1 (8.6%) separates N’Dama from the two European breeds. PC2 (5.0%) separates Angus from Holstein. That matches what we know about cattle history: the African taurine N’Dama is the most distinct.
ANG_066, recorded as Angus, sits inside the Holstein cloud. It is a mislabelled Holstein.
HOL_077, recorded as Holstein, sits halfway between Holstein and N’Dama. It is a crossbred: a 50:50 cross falls in the middle of the line between its two parent breeds.
PC3 (0.8%) spreads out some Holsteins. Step 6 shows why.

  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +                          # 2
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +              # 3

section: 11.8 Step 6: watch out for families and duplicates
text:
11.8 Step 6: watch out for families and duplicates
A group of close relatives can take over a PC of its own, a problem described in many GWAS teaching notes (see Appendix C). It happened to our PC3: the animals with extreme PC3 scores were all members of a few Holstein families (F01, F14, F07, F11), because a sire, a dam and two calves share a lot of genome. PC3 described families, not breeds.
The fix is to compute the PCs on unrelated animals only and then project everyone else onto those PCs, using the SNP loadings. PLINK 2.0 does both steps:
# 1. PCs from the 301 founders only, saving the SNP loadings
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --keep founders.txt \
       --maf 0.05 --freq --pca 10 allele-wts --out pcaF
# 2. project all 361 animals onto those PCs
plink2 --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --read-freq pcaF.afreq \
       --score pcaF.eigenvec.allele 2 6 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize \
       --score-col-nums 7-16 --out proj






Figure 11.4: Left: PCs computed on all animals; family members (orange) stretch PC3. Right: PCs computed on founders only, with everyone projected. The families now sit inside their breed.



In the right panel the families sit neatly inside their breed. But two animals now stand far out on PC3: HOL_050 and HOL_050_rep, the duplicate sample from Chapter 10. Two identical “founders” are the most extreme family possible. So the rule is: remove duplicates and relatives first, then compute PCs, then project.

title: 11  Population structure and principal component analysis
text:
11.9 Step 7: check the SNP loadings
The loadings tell you which SNPs build each PC. For population structure they should be spread along the whole genome. A single tall peak means one region (often a large inversion or a region under strong selection) is driving the PC, and your LD pruning was not enough.






Figure 11.5: Absolute PC1 loadings along the genome. They are spread evenly, so PC1 reflects genome-wide breed differences.

section: 11.10 PCA and MDS: two roads to the same map
text:
11.10 PCA and MDS: two roads to the same map
An older alternative to PCA is multidimensional scaling (MDS) of the pairwise distances between animals. PLINK can do it directly:
plink --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --cluster --mds-plot 4 --out mds
# or: MDS in R from a PLINK distance matrix
d   <- as.matrix(read.table("dist.mdist"))          # plink ... --distance-matrix --out dist
ids <- read.table("dist.mdist.id")
mds <- cmdscale(d, k = 5, eig = TRUE)
pct <- round(mds$eig / sum(mds$eig) * 100, 2)      # here all eigenvalues are available
MDS works on IBS distances and PCA on the GRM. In our data both gave the same picture: three tight clouds, ANG_066 with the Holsteins and HOL_077 in the middle. PCA is faster for big data and is the standard choice for covariates, and the PLINK 2.0 --pca approx option handles tens of thousands of animals.

11.11 Using clustering to name the groups
PCA shows structure; clustering assigns animals to groups. --cluster --K 3 split our animals into 79 Angus; 141 Holsteins plus ANG_066; and 140 N’Dama, with HOL_077 in the Holstein cluster. Chapter 17 shows how --ppc and --mc change the clusters. For admixture proportions (for example, what share of HOL_077 is N’Dama), use ADMIXTURE on the pruned PLINK files.

title: 12  Case/control association
text:
12.1 Step 1: the allelic test
From here on we use the cleaned file cattle_qc (351 animals, 4,443 SNPs; Chapter 19 lists the QC steps). The disease is BRD: 138 cases and 213 controls. Every command starts with plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex.
Count alleles in cases and controls and put them in a 2 × 2 table. For our true BRD SNP:
The A allele makes up 62% of case chromosomes but only 40% of control chromosomes. The chi-square test (1 degree of freedom) asks whether a difference that large could easily happen by chance. The odds ratio summarises the size of the effect:
\[
OR = \frac{171/105}{168/254} = 2.46
\]
The odds of carrying A are 2.46 times higher on a case chromosome than on a control chromosome.
Something is very wrong: hundreds of SNPs have p-values below 10⁻¹⁰, and the true BRD SNP is only 238th.

title: 12  Case/control association
section: 12.2 Step 2: spot stratification with λ, the Manhattan plot and the QQ plot
text:
12.2 Step 2: spot stratification with λ, the Manhattan plot and the QQ plot
BRD is far more common in Holsteins (84 of 141) than in N’Dama (6 of 80). Any SNP whose frequency differs between those breeds therefore looks associated with BRD. This is population stratification, the most common cause of false positives in livestock studies.
The genomic inflation factor λ measures it. If almost no SNP is truly associated, the median chi-square across the genome should be 0.455 (the median of a chi-square with 1 degree of freedom):
\[
\lambda = \frac{\text{median}(\chi^2_{\text{observed}})}{0.455}
\]
λ near 1.0 is healthy, above 1.05 to 1.1 deserves attention, and 10.2 is a disaster.






Figure 12.1: Manhattan plots for BRD. Each dot is a SNP; height is -log10(p); the dashed line is the Bonferroni threshold. Top: naive test. Bottom: logistic regression with PC1 and PC2 as covariates.









Figure 12.2: QQ plot: observed against expected -log10(p). Under no association the points follow the line. The naive test (orange) climbs off the line from the start, the sign of inflation; the corrected test (blue) follows the line until the one true signal.

12.4 Step 4: other tests for the same question

12.4.1 Fisher’s exact test
The chi-square test is an approximation that becomes unreliable when a table cell has fewer than about 5 counts (rare SNPs, small studies). Fisher’s exact test computes the exact probability:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --assoc fisher --out a_fisher
For snp00706 it gave p = 1.36 × 10⁻⁸, close to the chi-square’s 1.04 × 10⁻⁸, because the counts are large.


12.4.2 Genotype models: trend, dominant, recessive and general
The allelic test counts alleles. --model counts animals by genotype and asks several questions at once:

Read AFF 50/71/17 as: among cases, 50 AA, 71 AC and 17 CC. TREND and ALLELIC are strongest, which fits an additive effect (each copy of A adds the same amount of risk), and that is how the SNP was simulated. GENO, DOM and REC are only computed when every cell has at least 5 animals; --cell 0 removes that rule.


12.4.3 Model comparison: is the effect additive?
--logistic --genotypic fits two terms per SNP: ADD (0, 1 or 2 copies of A1) and DOMDEV (1 for heterozygotes, 0 otherwise). DOMDEV measures how far the heterozygote is from halfway between the two homozygotes.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --logistic --covar pcs.txt --genotypic --out lg_geno
   5   snp00706   62019439    A        ADD      349      3.325        5.573    2.505e-08
   5   snp00706   62019439    A     DOMDEV      349      1.026      0.09652       0.9231
   5   snp00706   62019439    A   GENO_2DF      349         NA        31.19    1.688e-07
DOMDEV p = 0.92: no sign of dominance, so the simpler additive model is right. The fitted dominant and recessive models were weaker (p = 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ and 3.3 × 10⁻⁶).






WarningOR = inf



One SNP in this run reported OR = inf with p = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰³. An infinite odds ratio means one genotype appears only in cases or only in controls (“complete separation”), and the regression breaks. Always look at the genotype counts (--model) before believing such a result.




12.4.4 Stratified tests: Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel and Breslow-Day
Instead of a regression, you can split animals into strata (breeds) and combine the 2 × 2 tables:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --mh --within breed.clst --out mh
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --bd --within breed.clst --out bd
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --homog --within breed.clst --out homog
The CMH test asks whether there is an association within strata and gives one common OR: for snp00706, OR = 2.92 (95% CI 2.01 to 4.25), p = 9.9 × 10⁻⁹, with λ = 1.03. The Breslow-Day test asks whether the OR is the same in every stratum (p = 0.59, so yes). --homog shows each breed:

title: 13  Families, quantitative traits, interaction and permutation
text:
13.1 Quantitative traits
For a trait like weaning weight (WWT), PLINK fits a straight line: weight against the number of copies of allele A1 (0, 1 or 2). The slope, BETA, is the average change in kilograms per copy.
\[
\text{WWT} = \mu + \beta \times (\text{copies of A1}) + \text{covariates} + \text{error}
\]
You do not pick “case/control” or “quantitative” yourself: PLINK looks at the phenotype. If it only contains 1, 2 and missing, it is case/control; otherwise it is quantitative. The same --assoc flag then writes .assoc or .qassoc.

title: 13  Families, quantitative traits, interaction and permutation
text:
13.2 SNP-by-environment interaction
Does a SNP’s effect depend on the environment? In the simulation, snp01540 adds weight only in the feedlot.






Figure 13.3: Weaning weight (as deviation from breed mean) by genotype at snp01540, on pasture and in the feedlot. The lines are parallel if there is no interaction; here only the feedlot line slopes.



--interaction adds a SNP × covariate term for every covariate, and --parameters keeps only the terms you want. The numbering is: 1 = ADD, then the covariates in file order (2 to 6), then ADD × each covariate in the same order (7 to 11). So ADD × FEEDLOT is 10.
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT \
      --linear --covar cov_all.txt --interaction --parameters 1-6,10 --out lin_int
  10   snp01540   52104483    T         ADD      347    -0.3653      -0.2039       0.8385
  10   snp01540   52104483    T     FEEDLOT      347      23.19        7.813    7.086e-14
  10   snp01540   52104483    T ADDxFEEDLOT      347     -10.51       -4.051    6.322e-05
On pasture (FEEDLOT = 0), the T allele does nothing (BETA -0.37, p = 0.84). In the feedlot, each T allele costs an extra 10.5 kg (p = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵; 12 kg was planted).
PLINK 1.9 also has --gxe, which fits the SNP separately in two groups and compares the slopes:
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT --gxe --covar env.txt --out gxe
env.txt gives each animal a group (1 or 2). Across all breeds, --gxe gave p = 0.13, because it cannot include other covariates and breed differences blur the slopes. Within Holsteins only, the slopes were 0.34 kg (pasture) and -11.5 kg (feedlot), p = 0.0096. So prefer --linear --interaction with covariates; for case/control traits use --logistic --interaction. Chapter 16 adds continuous environments.

13.4 Family-based tests

13.4.1 The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT)
A heterozygous parent (Aa) passes A or a to a calf with a 50:50 chance, whatever its breed. If sick calves received A much more than half the time, A is linked to the disease. Because the comparison is inside the family, breed differences cannot fool it.
\[
\chi^2_{TDT} = \frac{(T - U)^2}{T + U}
\]
where T is the number of times A was transmitted from a heterozygous parent to an affected calf, and U the number of times it was not.

The direction is right (OR = 2) but p = 0.10: our 30 families give only 24 informative transmissions. A TDT needs hundreds of trios. Options: --tdt poo splits transmissions by parent of origin (11:5 from sires, 5:3 from dams here), --tdt exact gives exact p-values, --tdt perm empirical ones.

13.5 Asymptotic and empirical p-values
A normal (asymptotic) p-value comes from a formula that assumes a large sample and a well-behaved test. A permutation test makes no such assumption: it shuffles the phenotypes among the animals many times, recomputes the test each time, and asks how often a shuffled result beats the real one.








Option
What it does
Output




--perm
Adaptive: stops early for SNPs that are clearly not significant
EMP1, NP (permutations used)


--mperm 1000
Exactly 1,000 permutations, with genome-wide correction
EMP1, EMP2


--seed 1
Makes the shuffling repeatable





EMP1 is the empirical p-value for that SNP alone.
EMP2 is corrected for testing all SNPs. In each permutation PLINK keeps the largest statistic across the genome (“max(T)”), and EMP2 is how often that maximum beats this SNP’s real statistic. It is like Bonferroni but accounts for LD.
With N permutations, the smallest possible EMP1 is 1/(N + 1): 0.000999 with 1,000 permutations.

plink ... --logistic --covar pcs.txt --hide-covar --mperm 1000 --seed 1 --out lg_mperm

title: 14  Haplotypes, proxy association and imputation
text:
14.1 What PLINK has to guess: phase
We work on one small region around the BRD SNP, cut out with PLINK 1.9:
Genotypes do not tell you which alleles sit together on the same chromosome copy.
An animal that is A/C at one SNP and G/T at the next could carry its alleles in two ways:
Both give exactly the same genotypes (A/C and G/T), so the chip cannot tell them apart. PLINK uses the EM algorithm: it starts from a guess of the haplotype frequencies in the population, works out how likely each phase is for each animal, updates the frequencies, and repeats until nothing changes. Every phase with probability at least 0.01 is kept as a weighted possibility, and haplotypes rarer than 1% are dropped (--mhf 0.01). Calves are phased with the help of their parents.
You tell PLINK which SNPs make up each haplotype:

14.3 Is it one SNP or the whole haplotype? --chap
A haplotype signal raises two questions:

Does one SNP explain all of it?
Does that SNP matter on its own, or only through its neighbours?

--chap answers both by comparing two models. In the alternative model every haplotype has its own effect. In the null model some haplotypes are forced to share one effect. If forcing them together costs little, the simpler explanation is enough.

# 2. is anything left once we allow for snp00706?

14.5 Imputation: filling in SNPs you did not genotype
Suppose your animals were typed on a smaller chip than a reference group. The reference animals show which haplotypes go with which alleles at the missing SNPs, so the missing genotypes can be predicted from the neighbours.

A common CNV (a copy number polymorphism, CNP) can sit on top of a SNP. An animal can then carry, say, one A allele on one chromosome and a deletion on the other, which normal genotype calling reports as “AA”. PLINK 1.07 stores such data as generic variants in a .gvar file with copy numbers for each allele:
ANG ANG_001 ccnv1 A 1 G 0      # one A copy, the other chromosome deleted
ANG ANG_002 ccnv1 A 1 G 1      # normal heterozygote

PLINK 1.9 and 2.0 have no CNV commands. For livestock CNV work today: call CNVs with PennCNV (chips) or a sequencing caller, merge them into CNV regions with tools such as CNVRanger (R/Bioconductor), and test common regions by coding each animal’s copy number as a dosage or covariate in plink2 --glm.

text:
16.2 Epistasis: SNP × SNP interaction
Sometimes two SNPs only matter together. An epistasis test fits, for each pair, a model with both SNPs and their product, and tests the product term.
The BRD simulation included an epistatic pair, but it was built so that nearly every animal carried the risk combination, so it behaved like a single-SNP effect and the pair test failed (p = 0.57). Real epistasis is often just as hard to see. To show what a detectable interaction looks like, we simulated a second disease, PKE, caused only by the combination of snp01294 (chromosome 8) and snp03388 (chromosome 22).






Figure 16.1: Share of PKE cases for each two-SNP genotype. Risk is high in two opposite corners and low in the other two, so each SNP on its own averages out to nothing.



Single-SNP tests miss it completely:
   8   snp01294   ...  CHISQ 0.8231   P 0.3643   OR 0.87
  22   snp03388   ...  CHISQ 2.893    P 0.08894  OR 0.76

text:
16.3 SNP × environment with a continuous environment
Chapter 13 tested a two-level environment (feedlot or pasture). For a continuous one (age at weaning, temperature-humidity index, rainfall) you use the same --interaction, with one trap. Our first try with AGE in days gave NA for every SNP. The interaction column ADD × AGE (values near 0, 205 or 410) is almost a copy of ADD × 205, so it is nearly collinear with ADD, and PLINK’s collinearity check (--vif, default 50) rejects the model.
The fix is to centre the environment, which also makes the ADD term easier to read (it becomes the SNP effect at the average age):
# AGE_C = (AGE - 205) / 10
plink ... --linear --covar cov_c.txt --covar-name PC1,PC2,SEX_M,FEEDLOT,AGE_C \
          --interaction --parameters 1-6,11 --out int_agec
  10   snp01540   52104483    T        ADD      347      -5.29       -3.932    0.0001021
  10   snp01540   52104483    T  ADDxAGE_C      347     0.4663       0.4362        0.663
The feedlot SNP’s effect does not change with age (p = 0.66), which is correct: no age interaction was planted. Across the genome, 1 of 4,443 ADD × AGE_C terms had p < 0.001, close to the 4 expected by chance.

Our first centred version, AGE − 205, gave the value -9 to calves weaned at 196 days, and PLINK silently treated them as missing (NMISS fell from 347 to 336). Dividing by 10 avoided it. --missing-phenotype changes the missing code.

16.4 Meta-analysis: combining several studies
Each breed (or country, or research group) runs its own analysis and shares only the summary results. A meta-analysis combines them, giving more weight to the more precise estimates. The fixed-effect estimate is
\[
\hat\beta_{\text{meta}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \hat\beta_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{SE_i^2}
\]
Step 1: one analysis per breed, with the same A1 allele everywhere (--keep-allele-order) and standard errors (--ci 0.95):
for b in ANG HOL NDA; do
  plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --allow-no-sex --pheno pheno.txt --pheno-name WWT --keep-allele-order \
        --keep k_$b.txt --linear --covar cov_all.txt --covar-name SEX_M,FEEDLOT,AGE --hide-covar --ci 0.95 --out mk_$b
done
Step 2: combine them.
plink --cow --meta-analysis mk_ANG.assoc.linear mk_HOL.assoc.linear mk_NDA.assoc.linear + qt --out meta_fixed

Figure 18.1: Real cattle. Left: inbreeding coefficient F from --het, with lines at 3 standard deviations from the mean. Middle: PC1 against PC2. Right: genomic inbreeding from runs of homozygosity.



What the three panels say:

Heterozygosity. F averages 0.001 (SD 0.049), as expected when F is measured against the population’s own allele frequencies. Six bulls lie above +3 SD (F = 0.15 to 0.19). None lies below −3 SD, so there is no sign of contaminated samples. High F in a real herd usually means real inbreeding, not a lab error: these bulls should be checked, not removed.
PCA. PC1 and PC2 explain only 1.7% and 1.4% of the variation (eigenvalue divided by the GRM trace, 501.4; Chapter 11). Compare 8.6% in the simulated three-breed data. There are no separate clouds: this is one breed. The fan shape is typical of a population in which some groups of animals are more closely related than others. With no breed structure, the first PCs often pick up families, so in a GWAS of these bulls a mixed model with the GRM (GCTA, or plink2 --glm with PCs plus a relatedness check) would be safer than PCs alone.
ROH. All 500 bulls carry runs of at least 2 Mb, 4,346 runs in total. F_ROH averages 0.079 (maximum 0.258). The SNPs here cover about 1,048 Mb, so F_ROH is the share of that covered length. The three bulls with the most ROH (ID11528, ID11530, ID11593) are also among the six with the highest F, and across all bulls F and total ROH length correlate at 0.83: two different measures tell the same story.

Figure 18.2: Real sheep: PC1 separates Jacob from Navajo-Churro.



PC1 explains 9.7% of the variation and splits the two breeds cleanly; PC2 (4.8%) and PC3 (4.3%) describe spread within breeds. FST measures how much of the genetic variation lies between the breeds rather than within them:
\[
F_{ST} = \frac{\text{variance of allele frequency between breeds}}{\text{total variance}}
\]
PLINK computes the Weir and Cockerham estimator for every SNP. The log reports a mean FST of 0.142 and a weighted FST of 0.168: about 15% of the variation separates Jacob from Navajo-Churro. For comparison, FST between European cattle breeds is often around 0.05 to 0.15. Single SNPs with very high FST are candidates for selection signatures, which is a whole topic of its own.
ROH tell a breed story too (Figure 10.3): Jacob sheep carry on average 52.9 Mb of ROH on the two chromosomes (F_ROH about 0.18 of the 291 Mb covered), against 27.0 Mb (about 0.09) in Navajo-Churro.

plink --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --genome --min 0.2 --out ibd   # Chapter 10
plink --bfile cattle --cow --extract prune.prune.in --maf 0.05 --pca 10 header tabs --out pca  # Chapter 11

# 1. Build the lists from those results (by reading the outputs and plots)
#    remove_animals.txt : 6 poor-DNA animals, contaminated ANG_030, duplicate HOL_050_rep,
#                         calf with the wrong sire HOL_F03_C2, crossbred HOL_077
#    sex_update.txt     : 4 animals set to their genetic sex
#    snp_exclude.txt    : 12 SNPs failing HWE (p < 1e-6) in any breed
#                         + 8 SNPs with --test-missing p < 1e-4
#    breed_fixed.clst   : ANG_066 relabelled as HOL

# 2. Apply them: animals first, then SNPs

plink --bfile step1  --cow --exclude snp_exclude.txt --geno 0.05 --make-bed --out step2
plink --bfile step2  --cow --mind 0.05 --make-bed --out step3
plink --bfile step3  --cow --maf 0.01 --make-bed --out cattle_qc

# 3. Structure for the association models
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --autosome --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out qc_prune
plink --bfile cattle_qc --cow --extract qc_prune.prune.in --pca 10 header tabs --out qc_pca

--het, --genome

--logistic with PCs, --mh --within
Rank 238 naive, rank 1 after correction, p = 2.3 × 10⁻⁸ (Chapter 12)


Weaning-weight QTL snp02145 (PLAG1 region, +9 kg)
--linear with covariates, --dosage, meta-analysis
p = 0.93 naive, 9.7 × 10⁻¹¹ with covariates; 9.6 kg estimated (Chapter 13)


Weaning-weight QTL snp00891 (LCORL region, +5 kg)
--linear
p = 0.0019, rank 18: real but underpowered (Chapter 13)


Feedlot-only effect snp01540 (+12 kg in feedlot)
--linear --interaction
ADD × FEEDLOT = −10.5 kg, p = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵ (Chapter 13)


Epistatic pair for BRD (snp00210 × snp03131)
--epistasis
Not detected (p = 0.57): almost every animal carried the risk combination (Chapter 16)


Deletion hotspot on chr 7 near 40 Mb, and higher CNV burden in cases
CNV --mperm, --cnv-indiv-perm
34 cases against 6 controls, EMP2 = 0.0001; 4.30 against 2.95 CNVs per animal (Chapter 15)



Almost every planted problem was found, and the two that were not (four SNPs with a handful of random errors, and the weak epistatic pair) are the kind real studies also miss. That is the honest lesson of QC: it catches the big problems reliably and the small ones only sometimes, which is why replication matters.

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Term
Meaning




A1 / A2
The two alleles of a SNP in PLINK 1.9 files. Effect sizes (OR, BETA) are always for A1. By default A1 is the minor allele


Allele frequency, MAF
Share of chromosome copies carrying an allele; MAF is the frequency of the rarer one


Call rate / missing rate
Share of genotypes read successfully; call rate = 1 − missing rate


Case / control
Affected (coded 2) / unaffected (coded 1) animal for a yes/no trait


CNV
Copy number variant: a deleted or duplicated stretch of DNA


Covariate
An extra variable in a model (PCs, sex, herd, age) used to remove its influence


D, D′, r²
Measures of linkage disequilibrium between two SNPs (Chapter 9)


Dosage
Expected number of A1 copies after imputation, between 0 and 2


Eigenvalue
How much variation lies along a principal component


Eigenvector
The direction of a principal component; its values are the PC scores


EMP1 / EMP2
Empirical p-value from permutation / the same, corrected for all tests


Epistasis
Interaction between two or more loci


F (inbreeding)
Excess homozygosity compared with expectation


F_ROH
Share of the genome covered by runs of homozygosity


FST
Share of genetic variation that lies between populations


Founder / nonfounder
Animal with both parents unknown / animal with at least one parent in the data


GRM
Genomic relationship matrix: relationships between animals estimated from SNPs


HWE
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: genotype shares p², 2pq and q² under random mating


IBS / IBD
Identical by state (same alleles) / identical by descent (same ancestral copy)


Imputation
Predicting genotypes that were not measured, using a reference panel


KING
A relatedness method that does not need population allele frequencies


λ (lambda)
Genomic inflation factor: median test statistic divided by its expected value; close to 1 is good


LD pruning
Removing SNPs so that the remaining ones are not strongly correlated


MDS
Multidimensional scaling of pairwise distances; an alternative to PCA


Mendel error
A calf genotype that is impossible given its parents’ genotypes


OR / BETA
Odds ratio (yes/no trait) / regression slope (measured trait) per copy of A1


PCA
Principal component analysis: a few axes that summarise genetic differences between animals


Phase
Which alleles sit together on the same chromosome copy


PI_HAT
Estimated share of the genome two animals share IBD


Population stratification
False associations caused by differences in both allele frequency and trait between groups


ROH
Run of homozygosity: a long homozygous stretch inherited from a common ancestor


Strand flip
The same SNP reported from the opposite DNA strand (A/G becomes T/C)


TDT
Transmission disequilibrium test: a family-based association test


Wahlund effect
Fewer heterozygotes than expected when separate populations are pooled

C.5 A note on originality
The explanations, worked examples, numbers and figures in this book were written and produced for it, using its own simulated and public data. Standard formulas (Hardy-Weinberg, F, D and r², the GRM, KING, λ, FST) and standard cut-offs (such as the KING relationship categories) are given with their original references. Where a teaching idea is shared with the courses listed above, those courses are acknowledged here and in the Welcome page.
